NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Three weeks after an apparent misunderstanding sparked a confrontation, deadly Hindu-Christian riots continue unabated in the remote east Indian state of Orissa. Police officers chase away a protester in Mangalore, India, Monday. By Tuesday, about 20 deaths had been reported, said Praveen Kumar, the superintendent of police in the worst-affected Kandhamal district. The latest casualty is a police officer who died after an armed mob of about 400 to 500 mostly Hindus torched a police station in the district on Monday, Orissa state police said. Orissa's Director General of Police G.C. Nanda the policeman died when the mob opened fire at officers fleeing the burning building. The attack, he said, may have been in retaliation for arrests that police made in the ongoing communal fighting.  Watch more about the riots in India » . The attack came two days after police fired on a crowd to prevent it from attacking Christian residents. Between three and six people died in the shooting, CNN's sister network CNN-IBN reported. The violence spread to southern India over the weekend when vandals attacked 14 churches in an hour in the state of Karnataka Sunday, the network said. The Christian community in the Karnataka -- numbering about 2.5 million -- said right-wing Hindus are targeting them for opposing the violence in Orissa. By Tuesday, police had arrested about 140 people in connection with the riots, said Karnataka's Inspector General of Police A.M. Prasad. Sixty of them -- all Hindus -- were arrested for the church attacks, Prasad said. The rest, mostly Christians, were charged with disturbing the peace, he said. Orissa has historically been a tinderbox of Hindu-Christian tensions. Some Hindu groups view the work of Christian missionaries in the state with suspicion. They accuse missionaries of bribing or forcing Hindus into converting. The seeds for the current conflict were planted on August 23, when Hindu leader, Laxmananda Saraswati, and four others were killed in Kandhamal after 20 to 30 gunmen barged into a Hindu school and began shooting, the Orissa chief minister's office said. The authorities have not determined who killed Saraswati, but after the incident they detained five people who are Christians, said Sukanta Panda, spokesman for the chief minister. The government says the killings may have been the work of Maoist rebels -- investigators have many unanswered questions -- but some hardline Hindus blamed a Christian minority. They took to the streets in anger, rampaging through predominantly Christian neighborhoods, ransacking shops and torching houses. They chopped down trees to block roads, making it difficult for police to reach trouble spots. A Christian orphanage was set on fire. A 20-year-old woman, who was teaching children inside, burned to death. Christian residents fought back, and the clashes spread. Authorities imposed a night curfew in many towns and deployed state and federal forces in the troubled areas, Kumar -- the police superintendent -- said. Both sides said the violence has left Christian churches and Hindu temples razed to the ground. This is not the first time the simmering anger has boiled over in the state with deadly consequences. In 1999, a Hindu mob burned to death an Australian missionary, Graham Staines, and his two children while they slept inside their car. And last Christmas, clashing groups killed four people and burned several churches in the same Orissa district -- Kandhamal. Maoist rebels, who claim to be fighting for the poor and the dispossessed, have been battling the Indian government in an insurgency that has resulted in thousands of casualties since the late 1960s. Some Christians accept the Maoist theory, saying the rebels have also struck against hard-line Hindus because they associate them as being closely aligned with the government. But Hindu groups insists that Christians were behind Saraswati's death. Unlike Orissa, Karnataka has until now been spared the large-scale clash between Christians and Hindus. But now, many in the Christian community fear their calm and prosperous state may become another battleground between the two religions, CNN-IBN said. CNN's Harmeet Singh contributed to this report .

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Nearly a month after a seemingly minor dispute ignited violence, lethal clashes between Hindus and Christians show no signs of stopping in the isolated eastern Indian state of Orissa.

According to Praveen Kumar, who serves as police superintendent in the hardest-hit district of Kandhamal, roughly 20 people had lost their lives by Tuesday.

The most recent victim was a police officer, according to Orissa state police. He was killed on Monday when a crowd of between 400 and 500 individuals—predominantly Hindus—set fire to a police station in the district. Orissa's Director General of Police, G.C. Nanda, explained that the officer died as the mob shot at police who were escaping the blazing building. Nanda suggested the assault might have been payback for arrests carried out by police during the continuing sectarian violence.

This incident took place just two days after officers had opened fire on a gathering to stop it from assaulting Christian locals. Somewhere between three and six individuals were killed in that shooting, as reported by CNN-IBN, CNN's affiliate network.

Over the weekend, the unrest reached southern India, where attackers struck 14 churches within a single hour in the state of Karnataka on Sunday, the network reported. Karnataka's roughly 2.5 million Christians claim that Hindu extremists are singling them out because they have spoken against the Orissa violence.

Karnataka's Inspector General of Police, A.M. Prasad, stated that around 140 individuals had been taken into custody in relation to the riots by Tuesday. Of these, 60—all Hindus—faced arrest over the church assaults. According to Prasad, the remainder, primarily Christians, were accused of disrupting public order.

The state of Orissa has long been a hotbed of hostility between Hindus and Christians. Certain Hindu organizations regard the activities of Christian missionaries there with distrust, alleging that these missionaries either pay off or coerce Hindus to change their faith.

The roots of the present unrest trace back to August 23, when a Hindu leader named Laxmananda Saraswati, along with four others, was slain in Kandhamal. The chief minister's office in Orissa reported that between 20 and 30 armed men stormed a Hindu school and opened fire. Officials have yet to identify Saraswati's killers, but they took five Christians into custody following the event, according to Sukanta Panda, the chief minister's spokesman.

While the government has indicated that Maoist insurgents may have carried out the murders—and investigators still have numerous unresolved questions—certain militant Hindus pointed the finger at the Christian minority. Enraged, they poured into the streets, storming through mostly Christian areas, looting stores, and setting homes ablaze. They felled trees to obstruct roadways, hindering police access to the affected zones. In one instance, a Christian orphanage was torched, and a 20-year-old woman instructing children inside perished in the flames. Christian residents retaliated, and the confrontations escalated.

Kumar, the police superintendent, reported that officials had enforced overnight curfews across numerous towns and stationed both state and federal troops throughout the affected regions. Both communities reported that the violence had reduced Christian churches and Hindu temples to rubble.

This is not the first occasion on which the underlying tensions have erupted with fatal results in the state. Back in 1999, a Hindu crowd burned an Australian missionary, Graham Staines, and his two children to death as they slept in their vehicle. Additionally, during the previous Christmas, rival factions killed four individuals and set several churches ablaze in this very same Kandhamal district of Orissa.

Maoist insurgents, who profess to be championing the cause of the poor and marginalized, have been waging an armed struggle against India's government since the late 1960s, an insurgency that has produced thousands of casualties. Some Christians endorse the Maoist explanation, noting that the rebels have also attacked hardline Hindus, whom they view as strongly connected to the government. Hindu groups, however, maintain that Christians were responsible for Saraswati's killing.

In contrast to Orissa, Karnataka had so far avoided major confrontations between Christians and Hindus. Yet now, according to CNN-IBN, many within the Christian community worry that their peaceful and thriving state could turn into yet another arena for conflict between the two faiths.

CNN's Harmeet Singh contributed to this report.

New Delhi serves as the capital city of India, standing as a vibrant symbol of the nation's rich history, cultural diversity, and modern aspirations. Located in the northern part of the country, this bustling metropolis is home to millions of people and functions as the political and administrative center of one of the world's largest democracies.

New Delhi beautifully blends the old with the new. Ancient monuments and historic landmarks stand alongside contemporary architecture and modern infrastructure. Visitors can explore magnificent structures such as India Gate, the Red Fort, and Humayun's Tomb, each telling a unique story of the country's past. As the seat of the Indian government, New Delhi houses important institutions including the Parliament House, the President's residence (Rashtrapati Bhavan), and various government ministries. New Delhi remains an essential destination for anyone wishing to understand India. It captures the essence of a nation that honors its ancient heritage while embracing progress and innovation. Whether for business, tourism, or education, New Delhi continues to attract people from across the globe, cementing its place as a truly remarkable city.

# Religious Violence in Orissa Spreads to Neighboring States

**Deadly clashes between Hindu and Christian communities continue to escalate across eastern India**

Violence between Hindu and Christian communities in India's eastern state of Orissa has left dozens dead and thousands displaced, with the unrest now spreading to the neighboring state of Karnataka, authorities said.

The clashes erupted following the assassination of prominent Hindu leader Swami Laxmananda Saraswati, an 80-year-old leader of the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP), who was shot and killed along with four associates at his ashram in the Kandhamal district.

While Maoist rebels have claimed responsibility for the killing, several Hindu organizations have blamed local Christians, triggering waves of retaliatory violence across the region.

## Rising Death Toll

Officials report that the death toll has climbed into the dozens as mobs have targeted churches, homes, and religious institutions. Thousands of people have fled their villages, seeking shelter in relief camps and forested areas to escape the violence.

Numerous churches, prayer halls, and Christian homes have been set ablaze, while some Hindu properties have also been attacked in the ongoing unrest. Aid organizations report that displaced families face dire conditions in overcrowded relief camps.

## Violence Spreads to Karnataka

The unrest has not remained contained to Orissa. In Karnataka, attacks on churches and Christian institutions have been reported in multiple districts, prompting authorities to deploy additional security forces and impose curfews in affected areas.

Christian leaders have condemned the attacks and called on the government to provide greater protection for their communities. Hindu nationalist groups, meanwhile, have demanded a thorough investigation into Saraswati's murder.

## Government Response

State and federal authorities have deployed police and paramilitary forces to restore order, imposing curfews in the most volatile areas. Officials have appealed for calm and urged religious leaders on both sides to help defuse tensions.

Human rights organizations have called for an independent investigation into the violence and demanded accountability for those responsible for the attacks.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

---

**Note:** These events reference the real communal violence that occurred in Kandhamal, Orissa (now Odisha) in August 2008. For accurate historical details and current reporting, please consult verified news archives.

## The Kandhamal Violence (2007–2008)

The most significant episode of Hindu-Christian communal conflict in the region occurred in Kandhamal district:

**Timeline and Trigger:**
- Violence first erupted in December 2007
- A more severe wave began in August 2008 following the murder of Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati, a Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) leader, and four associates

Several underlying factors have contributed to tensions in the region:

**Religious Demographics:**

---

## Aftermath and Longer-Term Developments

- The events drew national and international attention, including responses from human rights bodies
- The violence prompted broader discussions about religious freedom and minority protection in India

**Sectarian Violence Spreads Across Two States as Kandhamal Burns**

NEW DELHI — Communal violence that erupted in the tribal district of Kandhamal in eastern Orissa spread to neighbouring Karnataka over the weekend, as mobs torched churches, attacked a police station and left a trail of destroyed homes across two states, officials said Sunday.

The unrest, now in its second week, was ignited by the killing of a prominent Hindu religious leader and four of his associates at his ashram in Kandhamal. Authorities have blamed Maoist rebels for the assassination, but Hindu nationalist groups have pointed the finger at the district's Christian minority, triggering waves of retaliatory attacks.

At least two dozen people have been killed and thousands displaced since the violence began, according to state officials, though relief workers say the true toll is likely higher. Many of the dead were burned in their homes or hacked to death as mobs moved through remote forest villages that are difficult for security forces to reach.

**Police Station Overrun**

In one of the most serious incidents, a crowd numbering in the hundreds surrounded and attacked a police station in the Kandhamal region, setting vehicles ablaze and forcing officers to open fire, police said. Several people were injured in the confrontation. The assault underscored the collapse of civil authority in parts of the district, where curfews have been imposed but often ignored.

Reinforcements, including paramilitary units, have been rushed to the area, but officials acknowledge that the rugged terrain and the scattered nature of the attacks have hampered efforts to restore order.

**Churches Targeted in Karnataka**

The violence took a new turn as it jumped to Karnataka in the south, where mobs attacked more than a dozen churches, prayer halls and Christian institutions over the weekend. Windows were smashed, religious statues destroyed and buildings set alight in the coastal districts, where tensions have simmered for months.

Church leaders accused hardline Hindu organisations of orchestrating the assaults and criticised the state administration, run by a Hindu nationalist government, for failing to provide adequate protection. State officials rejected the accusations, saying dozens of people had been arrested and additional forces deployed.

**National Reverberations**

The bloodshed has drawn national and international concern. Christian groups have called for a nationwide day of protest, and opposition politicians in New Delhi have demanded that the central government intervene. Federal authorities said they had dispatched additional paramilitary companies and were monitoring the situation closely.

Relief camps in Kandhamal are now sheltering thousands of frightened villagers, many of whom fled into surrounding forests before making their way to safety. Aid workers described dire conditions, with shortages of food, water and medicine.

Christians make up roughly two percent of India's overwhelmingly Hindu population of more than one billion, but relations between the communities in some regions have grown increasingly strained over disputes involving religious conversion.

As night fell over Kandhamal, columns of smoke were still visible above several villages. "We are living in fear," said one displaced resident at a relief camp. "We do not know when it will be safe to return home."

Officials warned that the coming days would be critical in determining whether the violence could be contained or would spread further.

# Deadly Religious Clashes Erupt in Eastern India, Multiple Casualties Reported

*By Staff Correspondent*

**BHUBANESWAR, India** — At least several people were killed and dozens injured as violence between Hindu and Christian communities swept through rural districts of eastern India this week, prompting authorities to deploy additional paramilitary forces and impose curfews in the worst-affected areas.

The clashes, which began after a disputed incident in a tribal-dominated region, have raised fresh concerns about communal tensions in a country that has periodically seen violence between religious groups.

"We have deployed additional police forces and paramilitary units to restore order," a senior district police official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to brief the media. "Curfew has been imposed in the most sensitive areas, and we are appealing for calm on all sides."

Local authorities said homes and places of worship were among the structures damaged during the unrest, and that a number of families had fled to relief camps set up by the administration.

"The situation is tense but under control," a police spokesman told reporters. "We are investigating the circumstances that triggered the violence and will take action against anyone found responsible, regardless of their community."

## Maoist Involvement Alleged

Officials have raised the possibility that Maoist rebels, known locally as Naxalites, may have sought to exploit the unrest. The insurgents, who have waged a decades-long armed struggle across a swath of central and eastern India they call the "Red Corridor," have historically operated in impoverished tribal areas where state presence is weak.

"We are examining whether extremist elements played a role in escalating the situation," the district official said. "These areas have a history of Maoist activity, and such groups have been known to take advantage of local grievances."

The rebels, who say they are fighting for the rights of marginalized tribal communities and landless farmers, have been blamed in the past for inflaming existing social and religious divisions, though their exact role in the current violence remains unclear.

## Echoes of the Staines Killing

The latest violence has revived memories of one of India's most notorious cases of anti-Christian violence — the 1999 killing of Australian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons.

Staines, who had worked with leprosy patients in the region for decades, was burned alive along with his sons, aged 10 and 6, as they slept in their vehicle in a rural area. The killings drew international condemnation and shone a spotlight on tensions surrounding religious conversions in India's tribal belt.

A man was later convicted and sentenced in connection with the murders, in a case that became a symbol of the dangers faced by religious minorities in certain parts of the country.

## Background

India, a predominantly Hindu nation, is home to a small but significant Christian minority. Tensions have periodically flared over allegations of religious conversions, with Hindu nationalist groups accusing Christian missionaries of luring impoverished tribal communities to convert — charges that Christian organizations deny.

Religious minority groups have long called for greater protection, while officials insist they are committed to maintaining law and order and protecting citizens of all faiths.

Authorities said an investigation into the current violence was ongoing, and that the death toll could rise as reports continued to come in from remote areas.

# Communal Violence in Orissa Enters Third Week as Fears Grow of Spread to Southern India

## Religious clashes leave dozens dead, thousands displaced as tensions over conversions fuel unrest

**BHUBANESWAR, India** — Sectarian violence between Hindus and Christians has convulsed India's eastern state of Orissa for a third consecutive week, leaving dozens dead, churches and homes in ruins, and tens of thousands of people sheltering in relief camps and forests, according to state officials and aid organizations.

The unrest, concentrated in the impoverished Kandhamal district, has emerged as one of the most serious outbreaks of anti-Christian violence in India in recent memory, drawing condemnation from religious leaders and prompting the central government to dispatch additional paramilitary forces to restore order.

## The Spark

The violence erupted following the killing of Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati, a prominent Hindu religious leader affiliated with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP), along with four of his associates. Hindu nationalist groups initially blamed Christians for the assassination, though a Maoist rebel group later claimed responsibility for the attack.

Despite the Maoist claim, hardline Hindu organizations mobilized quickly, and reprisal attacks against Christian communities spread through Kandhamal and surrounding areas within days.

## Casualties and Displacement

State authorities have confirmed dozens of deaths, though Christian organizations and human rights groups say the actual toll is significantly higher, alleging that many killings in remote tribal areas have gone unrecorded.

The violence has displaced an estimated 50,000 people, according to relief agencies. Many fled into surrounding forests to escape the mobs, while others crowded into government-run relief camps lacking adequate food, water, and medical supplies.

Reports have documented mob attacks in which victims were killed with machetes, homes were set ablaze, and dozens of churches, prayer halls, and Christian institutions were destroyed or damaged. Orphanages and convents were also targeted, and there were harrowing accounts of clergy and aid workers being assaulted.

## The Conversion Dispute

At the heart of the conflict lies a longstanding and bitter dispute over religious conversions. Hindu nationalist groups accuse Christian missionaries of using material inducements—money, education, and healthcare—to convert impoverished tribal peoples and lower-caste Hindus, known as Dalits.

Christian leaders reject these accusations, insisting that conversions are voluntary and that their charitable work serves marginalized communities long neglected by mainstream society. They argue that many converts are drawn to Christianity precisely because it offers an escape from the rigid hierarchies of the caste system.

The tensions are further complicated by economic competition. Many converts historically belonged to lower castes, and their embrace of Christianity has, in some cases, altered longstanding social and economic relationships—fueling resentment among some Hindu groups.

Orissa has an anti-conversion law on its books, one of several such statutes across Indian states that require official permission for religious conversions. Critics say these laws are used to harass Christian minorities, while proponents argue they prevent coercive proselytizing.

## Political Dimensions

The violence has exposed political fault lines. Orissa was governed at the time by a coalition that included the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the main Hindu nationalist party at the national level. Critics accused the state government of responding slowly and failing to protect vulnerable minorities.

Opposition leaders and Christian groups called on the central government to take stronger action, while Hindu nationalist organizations defended their positions and continued to raise the conversion issue.

## Fears of Spreading Violence

Perhaps most alarming to authorities are signs that the unrest is spreading beyond Orissa. Incidents of anti-Christian violence, including attacks on churches, have been reported in the southern state of Karnataka, raising fears of a wider wave of communal conflict across India.

Christian leaders have expressed deep anxiety that the tensions could ignite in other states with significant Christian populations or active Hindu nationalist movements. The reports from Karnataka have heightened concerns that Orissa's violence may serve as a catalyst for broader sectarian confrontation.

## National and International Response

The violence has drawn international attention, including expressions of concern from the Vatican and various human rights organizations. Within India, secular and religious leaders across faiths have appealed for calm and communal harmony.

India's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, and Christians constitute roughly 2.3 percent of the country's population of more than one billion. While communal violence in India has historically more often involved Hindu-Muslim tensions, the Orissa unrest has underscored the vulnerability of the Christian minority.

Government officials have pledged to restore order and provide relief to the displaced, but with tensions still high and mobs continuing to operate in remote areas, aid workers warn that the humanitarian situation remains dire.

As the crisis enters its third week, the fundamental disputes underlying the violence—over conversion, caste, economic competition, and religious identity—remain unresolved, leaving open the possibility of continued unrest in a region already scarred by bloodshed.
